identification.summary: BladedFeline is an Iran-aligned cyberespionage group named by ESET, which reports activity since at least 2017 against Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) officials, later expanding to Iraqi central government officials and a telecommunications provider in Uzbekistan [S1][S3][S4]. ESET assesses it is a subgroup of OilRig (APT34) [S1][S2][S3].
identification.firstObserved: ESET reports earliest known activity in 2017 (KRG officials); ESET discovered the group in 2023 via the Shahmaran backdoor used against Kurdish diplomatic officials [S1][S4].
identification.notes: The name BladedFeline is ESET's. Secondary coverage links the parent group OilRig to APT34 and Hazel Sandstorm (formerly EUROPIUM), but no source seen here shows Microsoft assigning BladedFeline its own name; Microsoft mapping is unverified [S3]. ESET's wording of the OilRig link differs between its blog (medium confidence) and newsroom release (high or 'very likely') [S1][S2]. Do not merge BladedFeline facts with other OilRig subgroups such as ShroudedSnooper/Storm-0861 [S6].

attribution.sponsor: Iran-aligned; ESET states BladedFeline is likely a subgroup of OilRig. No government attribution was found in the sources gathered [S1][S2].
attribution.confidence: ESET: medium confidence in its blog and social post that BladedFeline is a subgroup of OilRig; its newsroom release states a stronger 'high' or 'very likely' assessment. Treat as vendor assessment only [S1][S2][S5].
attribution.basis: ESET cites code similarity between the PrimeCache IIS module and OilRig's RDAT backdoor, and initial implants traced to OilRig tooling [S1][S2][S3].

objectives: Cyberespionage and long-term access to high-ranking Kurdish and Iraqi government officials; ESET expects the group to keep developing implants to maintain access [S1][S2][S4].

sectors: Government (Kurdistan Regional Government, Iraqi central government)
targeting.notes: Victims named by ESET are Kurdish diplomatic officials (2023), Kurdish and Iraqi government officials (2024), and a telecommunications provider in Uzbekistan; ESET reported further activity consistent with BladedFeline TTPs against the same Uzbek company in March 2025 [S1][S2][S3][S5].

capabilities.summary: Tools reported by ESET: Shahmaran backdoor (64-bit PE in the Startup directory, unencrypted C2 traffic, file transfer and command execution) [S3]; Whisper backdoor, which uses compromised Exchange webmail accounts, creates inbox rules, receives commands by email and returns results in encrypted attachments [S1][S3]; PrimeCache, a malicious IIS module triggered by HTTP requests with a predefined cookie header, used for commands and file exfiltration [S1][S3]; reverse tunnels Laret and Pinar; the Flog web shell; and implants Slippery Snakelet, Hawking Listener and P.S. Olala [S3][S5]. ESET could not confirm initial access; for Iraqi victims it suspects exploitation of an internet-facing web server to deploy web shells [S3]. Timestomping and spearphishing appear in the imported record but were not confirmed in the cited sources.

campaigns.name: Early KRG compromise
campaigns.summary: ESET's timeline begins with access to Kurdistan Regional Government officials' networks as far back as 2017 [S1][S3].

campaigns.name: Shahmaran against Kurdish diplomatic officials
campaigns.summary: ESET discovered the group when the Shahmaran backdoor was used against Kurdish diplomatic officials, followed by expansion to Iraqi government officials [S1][S4].

campaigns.name: Whisper and PrimeCache campaign
campaigns.summary: ESET observed Whisper, PrimeCache, tunnels and other post-compromise tools in networks of Kurdish and Iraqi officials and an Uzbek telecom provider; ESET's timeline runs to March 2024 [S1][S3][S5].

campaigns.name: Renewed Uzbekistan activity
campaigns.summary: ESET detected activity consistent with BladedFeline TTPs against the same Uzbek company [S3].

campaigns.name: ESET publication
campaigns.summary: ESET published 'BladedFeline: Whispering in the dark' on 5 June 2025 [S1][S2].

campaigns.name: New infrastructure (Q2-Q3 2025)
campaigns.summary: ESET's APT report for April-September 2025 says BladedFeline set up new infrastructure in that period [S7].

diamond.adversary: Iran-aligned espionage group, assessed by ESET as an OilRig subgroup [S1][S2].
diamond.capability: Shahmaran, Whisper (Exchange-mailbox C2), PrimeCache (IIS module), Laret and Pinar tunnels, Flog web shell [S1][S3].
diamond.infrastructure: Compromised Exchange webmail accounts and IIS servers on victim networks used as C2 channels; new infrastructure set up in 2025 (details not seen) [S1][S3][S7].
diamond.victim: Kurdish and Iraqi government officials, diplomatic officials, and an Uzbek telecom provider [S1][S3].
diamond.socioPolitical: Iran-aligned collection of political and government information in Iraq and the Kurdistan Region [S1][S2].
diamond.technology: Internet-facing web servers, IIS and on-premises Exchange mail servers [S1][S3].

gaps: ESET's primary article and newsroom release could not be fetched (host unreachable); details rely on search-result summaries and secondary coverage [S1][S2].
Confidence in the OilRig link is stated inconsistently (medium vs high or 'very likely'); the exact wording in ESET's current text is unverified [S1][S2].
Initial access vector is unconfirmed by ESET [S3].
No Microsoft or MITRE name mapping for BladedFeline was found; the imported MITRE group id is empty.
Spearphishing, T1190 exploitation and timestomping in the imported summary are not confirmed by the sources gathered.
ESET's 2025 new-infrastructure detail and any activity after 2025 are not available in the sources gathered [S7].
Whether secondary reports mentioning 'Spearal' tooling reflect ESET's text was not verified.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is internet-facing IIS and Exchange servers and the mailboxes of government and diplomatic officials in Iraq and the Kurdistan Region, plus regional telecom providers [S1][S3]. STEP 2: The actor persists quietly for years in government networks and uses mail and web services as C2 to blend with normal traffic [S1][S3]. STEP 3: Likely sequence is web-server compromise and web shell, then Whisper or PrimeCache, then tunnels for persistence and collection [S3]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued collection against Iraqi and Kurdish officials and regional telecoms. MDCOA is use of telecom or webmail footholds to reach partner-nation communications relevant to coalition activity; this is analyst speculation, not sourced. Candidate indicators: unexpected inbox rules on Exchange accounts, odd cookie-header requests to IIS, unknown IIS modules, and web shells such as flogon.aspx [S1][S3].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track ESET and partner reporting on Iran-aligned actors in Iraq and Central Asia; vendor-only attribution means low-to-moderate fidelity [S1][S2]. (2) Authorities: any coalition or partner-nation support is a coordination and information-sharing matter, not a basis for action against actor infrastructure. (3) Mission assurance: audit IIS modules and Exchange mailbox rules on supported and partner-hosted systems [S1][S3]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with partner CERTs and DC3 through established channels.

provenance.importedSummary: BladedFeline is an Iran-aligned APT group that has been active since at least 2017, targeting Iraqi and Kurdish government officials for cyberespionage. The group employs a variety of tools, including the Shahmaran backdoor, Whisper, and PrimeCache, which is a malicious IIS module. BladedFeline utilizes techniques such as spearphishing (T1566), exploiting public-facing applications (T1190), and timestomping to maintain access and exfiltrate data. The group is assessed with medium confidence to be a subgroup of OilRig, focusing on strategic access to high-ranking officials in the region.
